collaboratively Hands-on experience in implementing numerical methods is highly desirable Previous experience in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is desirable, while experience in multiphase flow Doctoral Position for developing advanced magnetic concepts required in future high power grid interfaces Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position for developing advanced magnetic concepts required in future high power grid interfaces 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Laboratory for High Power Electronic Systems (HPE) at the Department of Information Technology and Electrical Engineering of ETH Zurich conducts internationally leading research on power electronic converter systems, which are required, for example, in future energy distribution systems for the integration of renewable energy sources or in traction applications/electric vehicles. Another research focus is on solid-state pulse modulators for medical applications (computer tomography/cancer treatment) and accelerators (CERN). For the design and optimisation of the various power electronic systems, we develop advanced multi-physics models/digital twins/virtual prototypes at the component and system level. For a new research project on high-power grid interfaces for future data centres, PV, and energy storage systems, we are looking for a: Doctoral Candidate (PhD position), with a workload of 100% of  for developing advanced magnetic concepts required in future high power grid interfaces Job description We are looking for highly motivated individuals with an outstanding academic background to pursue a Doctorate (PhD) in the multidisciplinary field of developing, modelling and optimising advanced magnetic devices (inductors, transformers and filters) for use in future high-power grid interfaces and active rectifiers These devices are essential for filtering and protection in grid interfaces and significantly impact the achievable system power density and efficiency Bidirectional grid interfaces connect the AC grid to the DC 'load', and potential applications include large-scale data centres, large-scale photovoltaic (PV) systems and battery energy storage systems for storing the fluctuating energy of renewable energy sources To maximise the efficiency and power density of these high-power grid interfaces, you will design new magnetic device concepts and develop multi-physics models that describe (HF) losses in the windings and cores, cooling/temperature distribution, parasitic capacitances, magnetic couplings between the different components, and electrical insulation In addition to designing the magnetic devices, you will work on optimising the modulation schemes and operation during grid failures of the grid interfaces, as these have a significant impact on the magnetics design The developed concepts and models will be integrated into optimisation procedures for power electronic converter systems in a computationally efficient way This is essential for achieving outstanding system efficiencies and power densities, as well as gaining a competitive edge The models are also part of an ongoing, wider modelling framework development project at HPE, offering the opportunity to collaborate with other Doctoral candidates (PhD candidates) on different modelling aspects For verifying the new concepts and developed models, you will design and Doctoral position in robotic spraying for biocementation Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral position in robotic spraying for biocementation 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Chair for Digital Building Technologies invites applications for a PhD position on robotic spraying as an additive manufacturing process for biocementation. The research brings together two closely coupled lines of work: the development of an additive robotic fabrication system based on material deposition and microbially induced calcium carbonate precipitation (MICP), with a focus on applying MICP to the fabrication of architectural elements. This PhD is part of the SNSF-funded project “DFabuLis: Digital Fabrication Using Living Systems”, conducted in collaboration with Dr. Dimitrios Terzis, Senior Scientist in the Laloui group at EPFL. Project background Conventional cement-based construction binds aggregates through an energy-intensive process. Bio-binders offer a different fabrication logic. In biocementation, certain bacteria precipitate calcium carbonate between particles, allowing binding to form under ambient conditions. This project treats the bio-binder as a fabrication parameter. Through robotic deposition of bacterial and cementation solutions, mineral binding can be spatially controlled across a printed structure, producing architectural elements with locally differentiated density, strength, porosity, and surface properties within a single component. The research will investigate how robotic deposition of biocement can be translated into architectural production strategies, from material placement and component geometry to surface formation and assembly. In collaboration with the Soil Mechanics Laboratory at EPFL, the project connects robotic fabrication with the characterisation and formulation of bio-binders. The resulting strategies will be explored in architectural-scale demonstrators. Job description You will develop a robotic fabrication process for biocementation, including adapting existing deposition hardware, and the computational workflow linking design intent to material placement You will use it to produce architectural components, investigating through making how graded biocementation can inform structure, surface, and assembly You will assess the environmental footprint of the process and use it to guide fabrication and design choices You will conduct research in close collaboration with project partners at ETH and EPFL and, where applicable, industry partners. You will work closely with the Soil Mechanics Laboratory at EPFL, whose characterisation of the material will inform the development of the process You will write scientific articles for publication in peer-reviewed journals, present at international conferences, and contribute to teaching through the supervision of semester and master's projects Profile A Master's degree in architecture or a closely related discipline, with a demonstrated body of work in digital fabrication Competence in building and modifying fabrication equipment; experience with robotics, electronics, or control software is a strong asset Fluency in computational design and experience moving between digital models and physical results Interest in biological or material processes; experience in a wet lab is welcome but not required. Two Doctoral Positions in the SNSF Research Project "From Homes to Habitat – Swiss Housing Cooperatives as Agents of Socio-Ecological Transition" Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Two Doctoral Positions in the SNSF Research Project "From Homes to Habitat – Swiss Housing Cooperatives as Agents of Socio-Ecological Transition" 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken ETH Wohnforum – ETH CASE (Centre for Research on Architecture, Society & the Built Environment) at the Department of Architecture, ETH Zurich, is seeking two doctoral researchers (100%, four years) to join the SNSF-funded research project “From Homes to Habitats – Swiss Housing Cooperatives as Agents of Socio-Ecological Transition,” starting on 1 June 2027 or upon agreement. The PhD will last from 2027-2031 (4 years). Project background How can housing support a shift towards more sustainable ways of living? The overall research project investigates the potential of housing cooperatives in Switzerland as agents of socio-ecological transition. Moving beyond their established role in providing affordable housing, the project examines how housing cooperatives develop innovative social, spatial, and ecological practices across diverse territorial contexts. While existing research has predominantly focused on housing cooperatives in major cities, the project investigates housing cooperatives in metropolitan, peri-urban, rural, peripheral, and Alpine territories, examining how different urbanisation processes shape cooperative housing practices and their potential for socio-ecological transformation. The project is hosted at ETH Wohnforum – ETH CASE, Department of Architecture, ETH Zurich, under the responsibility of Prof. Dr. Elli Mosayebi , Professor of Architecture and Design. The doctoral researchers will work within an interdisciplinary research team bringing together expertise in architecture, housing, urban and territorial studies, and socio-ecological transformation. In addition, you will benefit from being associated to the Doctoral Programme at the ETH Zurich Department of Architecture’s Institute of Landscape and Urban Studies (LUS). ETH Wohnforum – ETH CASE (Centre for Research on Architecture, Society & the Built Environment) is an interdisciplinary institute for research, consulting and education in the field of housing, architecture, and urban development at the department of architecture at ETH Zurich. Job description We are seeking two motivated doctoral researchers to join our interdisciplinary research team and contribute to the investigation of housing cooperatives as agents of socio-ecological transition across Switzerland. Your responsibilities and tasks will include: Contribute to the development of the project's conceptual and methodological framework. Participate in the mapping and typology building of housing cooperatives across Switzerland. Design and conduct qualitative case studies within the respective territorial focus. Undertake fieldwork, including site visits, interviews, participant observation, and spatial documentation. Analyse architectural, spatial, social, and ecological practices through qualitative and visual research methods. Participate in the organisation of workshops with researchers, housing cooperatives, and relevant stakeholders. Profile Master's degree in architecture, urban studies, sociology, or a related discipline, with a strong interest in housing, territorial transformation, and socio-ecological questions. Strong interest in interdisciplinary research at the intersection of architecture, society, and ecology. Renes and co-supervised by Renato Renner. Quantum computers promise capabilities far beyond today's computers, but only if we can reliably protect quantum information from errors. Quantum error correction (QEC) is therefore one of the central challenges on the path toward large-scale quantum computing. In this Doctoral project, you will investigate the fundamental limits of quantum error correction. The position is part of QuBriC , the first European Marie Skłodowska-Curie Doctoral Network (MSCDN) dedicated entirely to QEC, and includes secondments to Politecnico di Milano and Quantinuum in Cambridge, England. The PhD position is fully funded for 3 years. The expected starting date is early/mid 2027, but a later start is also possible. Job description Your main responsibility will be to conduct high-quality research within the project and progressively develop your own research ideas The exact direction of the project can be shaped according to your background and research interests You will perform numerical experiments and theoretical analysis, develop algorithms and software, and communicate your results through publications and presentations at leading international conferences and journals You will collaborate extensively with researchers within QuBriC and participate in the network's research, training, and dissemination activities. The position also includes teaching at the undergraduate and Master's level and other departmental duties, corresponding to up to 20% full time The position is a fixed-term appointment of three years, with a starting salary of 61’400.00 CHF per annum. Profile To qualify as a Doctoral student, you must have a Master's degree (or equivalent) in physics, mathematics, electrical engineering, computer science, or a closely related field. The following will strengthen your application: A strong mathematical background, with roots in either information theory or quantum information science Curiosity about the implications of quantum mechanics for information processing Motivation to deliver ambitious, high-quality work Ability to work independently as well as collaboratively in an international research environment Strong written and verbal communication skills in English Strong programming skills (e.g., Python, Matlab, or similar) Familiarity with classical and/or quantum coding theory, error correcting codes, and decoding algorithms Previous experience in research and teaching Because this position is funded through a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Doctoral Network, additional eligibility requirements apply. In particular: Candidates must not already hold a doctoral degree at the date of recruitment Mobility rule: The candiate must not have resided or carried out their main activity (work, studies, etc.) in Switzerland for more than 12 months in the 36 months immediately before their recruitment date Workplace Workplace We offer You will be part of a welcoming, open and interactive research group in the Institute of Theoretical Physics, working at the intersection of quantum information theory, quantum cryptography, and quantum foundations Our working language is English As part of QuBriC, you will join a cohort of 15 MSCDN doctoral candidates based in Europe's leading QEC groups, and you will meet them regularly at network-wide training schools, workshops and conferences chevron_right Working, teaching and research at ETH Zurich We value diversity and sustainability In line with our values , ETH Zurich encourages an inclusive culture. jobs.title: Doctoral Position: 3D scene reconstruction and multi-modal sensing for digital twins of stone-built heritage
jobs.description:
Doctoral Position: 3D scene reconstruction and multi-modal sensing for digital twins of stone-built heritage Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position: 3D scene reconstruction and multi-modal sensing for digital twins of stone-built heritage 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Chair of Geosensors and Engineering Geodesy at ETH Zurich is looking for a Doctoral candidate to work on 3D mapping, scene reconstruction and multi-modal sensing for information-rich digital twins of heritage buildings. The position is part of the collaborative project “HC3 – Heritage Conservation Collaboration Copilots”. HC3 aims to establish information-rich 3D digital twins of stone-built monuments that are interoperable through eXtended Reality (XR), together with the sensing and monitoring methods that provide the data they are built on. These will help us model and understand how stone-built heritage deteriorates, and predict how this deterioration will evolve under climate change. Within the project, you would collaborate with two other Doctoral students employed by the Chair of Physical Chemistry of Building Materials at ETH Zurich and a postdoctoral researcher working on the interface of both Chairs. The HC3 project is lead by Prof. Robert Flatt at Chair of Physical Chemistry of Building Materials and by dr. Tomislav Medic at Chair of Geosensors and Engineering Geodesy (Tomislav would be your direct supervisor). jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in Magnetic Resonance Applications in Porous Media Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in Magnetic Resonance Applications in Porous Media 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The ETH Zurich Geothermal Energy & Geofluids ( GEG.ethz.ch ) Group in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences investigates subsurface reactive fluid and geothermal energy transfer, developing and employing computer simulations, laboratory experiments, and field analyses. Our aim is to gain fundamental insights and develop sustainable technologies to address societal needs. The position is 100% with a competitive salary according to ETH Zurich standards. The position is for one year with the potential for annual extensions based on project needs and employee performance. The position start date is 1st of February 2027 or as soon as possible thereafter. Project background We are excited to announce a PhD opportunity focused on developing and applying multi-modal magnetic resonance techniques for studying chemical and physical processes in porous media (e.g., natural rock formations). The group is implementing state-of-the-art nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (NMR/MRI), electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR)-MRI, and dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) instrumentation. Fundamental processes will be probed in porous media including multicomponent fluid flow (e.g., H2O, and CO2), H2O-quartz-radical reactions, mineral precipitation, microbial methanogenesis, and crystalline hydration. Job description The PhD project will explore: Developing new methods and techniques in NMR/MRI, pulsed-EPR-MRI, and DNP Characterization of radical centers in natural rock samples with EPR spectroscopy and imaging Understanding DNP in porous media both with exogenous and endogenous radical sources Studying selected applied chemical and physical processes in porous media possibly including: Multicomponent fluid flow and temperature encoding Mechanochemical radical generation during rock fracturing and its role in water splitting to form hydrogen gas, oxygen gas, and reactive oxygen species Quantification of 13C-enriched CO2, bicarbonate, and/or CH4 in porous media through different phases and geochemical reactions Tracking mineral precipitation via 23Na and/or 7Li isotope handles The work will include method development of various magnetic resonance techniques with a focus on porous and fractured media. Applied projects will combine experimental stimulations (e.g., high-pressure fracture experiments), magnetic-resonance-based characterization, geochemical analysis, microbial ecology approaches, alongside modeling fluid migration and storage potential. Profile We seek a highly motivated and self-organized individual with: Background in chemistry, physics, engineering, or similar Strong interest in interdisciplinary research bridging chemistry, physics, geochemistry, geomechanics, microbiology, and energy science Experience with liquid- or solid-state NMR, MRI, or EPR Familiarity with analytical tools such as X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray computed tomography (XRCT) Experience in designing and performing high-temperature and high-pressure in-situ experiments is advantageous Fluency in English (both written and spoken) Workplace Workplace We offer We provide a dynamic and exciting work environment with cutting-edge computational and laboratory infrastructure at ETH Zurich in general and in the GEG group in particular. The GEG Group’s laboratory includes both low-field (~ 50 mT) and high-field (5.6 T) multinuclear NMR/MRI, pulsed-EPR-MRI, and DNP instruments. Further capabilities include an XRCT, laser Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV), and Laser-Induced Fluorescence (LIF). These are used to monitor reactive experiments, quantify, and visualize a wide range of components over varied temperatures and pressures in up to three spatial dimensions. jobs.description:
Doctoral Student in Magnetic Resonance for the Study of Granular Systems Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Student in Magnetic Resonance for the Study of Granular Systems 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken ETH Zurich is one of the leading universities worldwide and renowned for its excellence in education, fundamental and applied research, and technology transfer. At the Institute for Biomedical Engineering, one research focus is on nuclear magnetic resonance. The team of Prof. Klaas Prüssmann drives innovation in magnetic resonance from physical and mathematical principles all the way to novel imaging, sensing, and tracking technology. In close collaboration with academic and industrial partners, we pursue applications in the biomedical realm, process engineering, and materials science. One recent focus of interest is on the use of magnetic resonance for particle tracking in granular systems. We are looking for a Physicist or Engineer to join us on this frontier as a Doctoral Student. Project background Granular systems are ubiquitous in nature and of fundamental importance to industry, from food and pharma to material conversion. However, despite their widespread occurence and use, many important phenomena such as the transition between flowing and solid states, mixing, segregation, or surface instabilities, are poorly understood. Magnetic resonance has proven a powerful means of studying granular physics, permitting both dynamic imaging and, newly, the tracking of particle swarms. The focus is now on further expanding the tracking strategies and, in the applied realm, on exploring the role of the shape of particles and how granular dynamics change when particles are soft and deform upon stress. The project is a shared effort with ETH colleagues in process engineering and encompasses two Doctoral Student positions, one each at the Institute for Biomedical Engineering (Prof. Prüssmann) and the Laboratory of Energy Science and Engineering (Prof. Müller). The two Doctoral Researchers will benefit from immersion in both environments and are foreseen to collaborate closely. Job description The objective of the Doctoral Student hired by the Institute for Biomedical Engineering is to advance magnetic resonance technology and methods towards the study of granular systems made up of arbitrarily shaped and soft particles. This will include work on principles of particle tracking and imaging, creation of new methods, implementation on magnetic resonance equipment, all the way to  experimental exploration and use in granular systems. The collaborative effort with the partner Doctoral Student will particularly target the fabrication of tailored and soft particles, applied studies in granular systems science, and the creation of experimental setups to this end. Profile Applicants for this position are expected to have a Master’s degree in Physics, Electrical Engineering, or Mechanical Engineering, or from another program with substantial coverage of Physics and Mathematics. The position also requires a good command of English, both oral and written. We highly value: Analytical strength Intellectual rigor Creativity Passion for both abstract thought and practical implementation Intrinsic motivation Team orientation Previous experience with magnetic resonance or granular systems is a benefit but not a requirement. Our interdisciplinary approach includes the design and manufacturing of miniaturized platforms and their optimization for biochemical assays and analytical procedures. To strengthen our team, we are offering a Doctoral Position for developing an organ-on-chip model system. Project background Organ-on-chip systems, also known as microphysiological systems, are promising platforms for investigating disease development and evaluating potential treatments. jobs.title: Doctoral Position in Groundwater Microbial and Viral Ecology and Environmental Bioinformatics
jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in Groundwater Microbial and Viral Ecology and Environmental Bioinformatics Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in Groundwater Microbial and Viral Ecology and Environmental Bioinformatics 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Geomitigation of Greenhouse Gases group at ETH Zürich is actively recruiting a highly motivated and curious Doctoral candidate with a strong interest in environmental microbiology, biogeochemical cycling, and bioinformatics. The position is part of a newly funded SNSF interdisciplinary project investigating how microbial and viral communities influence carbon cycling in groundwater systems. The project brings together microbial and viral ecology, environmental genomics, and hydrogeochemistry to better understand how biological processes influence the fate of carbon in the subsurface. Project background Groundwater represents an important but poorly understood component of the global carbon cycle. While water-rock interactions strongly influence groundwater chemistry, microbial communities actively transform carbon through diverse metabolic pathways, and viruses may further regulate these processes through infection and metabolic reprogramming. However, how microbial and viral communities respond to changes in groundwater age and geochemistry, and how these interactions influence carbon cycling, remains largely unknown. In this project, you will investigate microbial and viral diversity, metabolic activity, and evolutionary adaptation across groundwater age gradients. By combining metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, and viral metagenomics with hydrogeochemical measurements, you will explore how microbial metabolism and virus-host interactions influence carbon cycling in the subsurface. Job description Analyze large-scale environmental metagenomic, metatranscriptomic, and viral sequencing datasets to investigate microbial and viral diversity, activity, and function in groundwater systems Characterize microbial metabolic potential and activity, with a particular focus on pathways involved in carbon cycling and their responses to environmental conditions Investigate microbial and viral community dynamics, virus-host interactions, and evolutionary adaptation across groundwater age and geochemical gradients Integrate environmental multi-omics datasets with hydrogeochemical measurements to better understand the biological processes influencing subsurface carbon cycling Perform DNA and RNA extractions from environmental samples and contribute to complementary laboratory analyses, including microbial cell abundance and activity measurements using flow cytometry and microscopy Synthesize research findings into scientific manuscripts and present results at international conferences and workshops Collaborate closely with the Principal Investigator, project partner, another Doctoral student working on groundwater hydrogeochemistry, and other group members while contributing to a supportive and communicative research environment Profile We are looking for a candidate who is curious, independent, and motivated by questions at the intersection of microbial ecology, evolution, and environmental biogeochemistry. You enjoy working with large biological datasets and are excited about using computational approaches to understand how microorganisms and viruses interact with their environments. An MSc degree in microbiology, microbial ecology, bioinformatics, computational biology, geobiology, or a closely related discipline Previous hands-on experience with metagenomic data analysis or closely related environmental bioinformatics approaches Experience working in Linux/Unix command-line environments and familiarity with computational biology workflows Experience with at least one programming or scripting language, such as Python, R or Bash A strong understanding of microbial ecology, physiology, and/or metabolism Excellent analytical and problem-solving skills, including the ability to work with complex biological datasets Creativity, curiosity, and motivation to explore new research questions and computational approaches Ability to work both independently and as part of a collaborative interdisciplinary team Excellent spoken and written English Experience with genome-resolved metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, comparative genomics, or high-performance computing is particularly advantageous. Previous experience with DNA and/or RNA extraction from environmental samples is also desirable. A background in groundwater microbiology, environmental geochemistry, or biogeochemical cycling is beneficial but not required. jobs.title: Doctoral Position in Environmental Microbiology
jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in Environmental Microbiology Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in Environmental Microbiology 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Environmental Microbiology group led by Prof. Marie Schölmerich at the Department of Environmental Systems Science, ETH Zurich, invites applications for a fully funded 4 year Doctoral Position. Our group explores the fascinating world of anaerobic microbiology from the global to the microscopic scale. This project investigates the physiology and bioenergetics of alkaliphilic methanogenic archaea. Project background The National Centre of Competence in Research NCCR Genesis is a research infrastructure project funded by SNSF focussing on exploring the emergence of life in the Universe. This interdisciplinary research infrastructure brings together physicists, earth and planetary scientists, chemists and biologists to understand the conditions and the mechanisms that enable life to emerge. Developing reliable methods to detect reliable traces of life (biosignatures) – whether through remote sensing or direct onsite measurements – requires significant innovation. These challenges demand close collaboration across physics, biology, chemistry and the earth sciences. NCCR Genesis does not aim to provide answers in all fields, but to drive innovative research and achieve decisive progress. Details on NCCR Genesis are available on its website . jobs.description:
Doctoral Student in Environmental Bioengineering Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Student in Environmental Bioengineering 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Environmental Microfluidics Group of Prof. Roman Stocker in the Institute of Environmental Engineering is seeking a dynamic and motivated doctoral student with an engineering background for a project on how bacterial chemotaxis accelerates plasmid transfer, including the spread of antibiotic resistance. The position is funded by a recently awarded SNSF grant, and the project is a joint effort with Prof. Jonasz Slomka at the University of Warsaw. This position will be based in the laboratory of Prof. Roman Stocker. Project background Bacterial conjugation, the contact-dependent transfer of plasmids between cells, speeds up bacterial evolution and is a major route for the spread of antibiotic resistance in the environment, which in turn poses a global health threat. Aquatic environments are full of microscale chemical hotspots, such as the nutrient-rich 'phycosphere' around phytoplankton and sinking marine particles, and chemotactic bacteria are known to find and accumulate rapidly at these locations. This project will test the hypothesis that this accumulation enhances plasmid spreading in the environment, contributing to a cutting-edge view of the role of antibiotic resistance in nature. The project seeks to study when, where and how strongly this enhancement operates across different chemical hotspots, fluid flows and bacterial strains, and what it means for the spread of antibiotic resistance among aquatic bacteria. Job description This is a primarily experimental PhD at the interface of engineering and microbiology. The student will: Design, build and characterize new instrumentation to couple existing chemotaxis assays to controlled shear systems. This includes mechanical design, 3D printing, control systems and integration with a fluorescence microscope. Run chemotaxis and conjugation experiments with bacterial donors and recipients of plasmids and a range of chemoattractants, with the opportunity to learn and use advanced techniques such as flow cytometry and plate-reader-based plasmid transfer quantification. Image and track fluorescently labeled bacteria and chemical plumes in shear flow, and analyze the data with quantitative image- and data-analysis pipelines. Test clinically relevant bacteria and freshwater (e.g. lake) bacteria, to assess the potential for chemotaxis-driven spread of resistance in the environment. Contribute data to mathematical models of plasmid spread. Profile We are looking for a hands-on, skilled and curious engineer who loves to build new tools and is interested in using them to answer fundamental scientific questions. Ideal candidates hold an MSc degree in bioengineering, mechanical engineering, mechatronics, electrical engineering, environmental engineering, physics or a related discipline, and have some (not necessarily all) of the following skills: Practical experience in prototyping and manufacturing, for example CAD, 3D printing, machining (strongly preferred). Experience with control systems and instrumentation, for example motor control, sensors, microcontrollers, and automation or data-acquisition code (Python, MATLAB, LabVIEW or similar) (preferred). Openness to gain experience in the microbiology laboratory: bacterial cultures, sterile technique, plate readers and flow cytometry. Familiarity with microscopy, image analysis, fluid mechanics or microfluidics (beneficial but not necessary). Fluency in English (oral and written), enthusiasm for working in an interdisciplinary and international team, and the drive to pursue scientific excellence (required). You will be guided by Prof. Roman Stocker and by members of his lab with extensive experience in microbiology, experimental techniques and environmental processes. You will have the opportunity to work in a cutting-edge, fast-paced research environment, interact with researchers from many different disciplines (engineers, physicists, microbiologists, oceanographers, chemists, mathematicians), gain technical experience across diverse research approaches and interact with world-class collaborators. jobs.description:
Doctoral Students in Quantum Networking with Superconducting Circuits Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Students in Quantum Networking with Superconducting Circuits 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Quantum Device Lab is looking for highly motivated Doctoral Students for the development of a superconducting qubit quantum network and research in quantum networking applications. A team of researchers led by Andreas Wallraff from the Quantum Device Lab , at the Department of Physics of ETH Zurich has developed a unique superconducting qubit system consisting of two dilution refrigerators equipped with superconducting qubit chips, separated by 30 meters, and connected through a cryogenic link. By exchanging microwave photons across the link, this system can generate remote entanglement between the separated chips as a resource for quantum information experiments and applications. The platform has already enabled demonstrations including loophole-free Bell tests and randomness amplification . We are now expanding the platform through advances in chip fabrication, packaging, networking protocols, and distributed control systems. These developments will enable research into further potential application areas of quantum networks, including loss-tolerant photonic state transfer, distributed quantum computing and quantum error correction, blind quantum computing, and non-local sensing. To ensure this project's success and fast progress, we are looking for highly motivated Doctoral Students in quantum networking with superconducting circuits. Job description You will become part of our team developing and running a two-node quantum network You will be working closely with the rest of the Quantum Device Lab, a well-established research group with a strong background in quantum computing with superconducting qubits, and be able to both benefit from the expertise developed there and contribute to its progress You will perform collaborative research towards the realization of quantum networking technologies You will get to contribute to diverse aspects of the experimental effort, both technical (design of electronics and mechanical components, building of microwave setups, fabrication of superconducting circuit chips) and conceptual (design of experiments, exploring quantum networking applications, planning of future research strategies) In the lab, you will pursue the development of the platform by enabling and implementing quantum networking protocols on a network of multi-qubit superconducting circuit chips Profile You have a strong interest in experimental realizations of quantum information processing systems, with a focus on remote and non-local applications You are dedicated to pursuing a successful career in research, development, or education, either in academia or industry You have experience and a proven record in one or more of the following: Quantum information processing and its implementations (e.g. with superconducting circuits, quantum dots, ion traps, NMR) Experimental quantum optics and atomic physics (cavity quantum electrodynamics) Micro and nano-electronic devices and their fabrication (lithography and deposition techniques) Quantum networking and remote entanglement generation Mesoscopic solid state physics Low temperature physics Microwave electronics Digital electronics FPGAs Instrumentation, drivers, and software development Workplace Workplace We offer Your project is embedded into the Swiss Quantum Science and Technology network, the Quantum Center at ETH Zurich, and into the broader context of a diverse set of international research projects. You will have the unique opportunity to contribute to a strong research program conducted at a leading European research institution. ETH Zurich provides a stimulating interdisciplinary research environment in quantum information science. jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in High Intensity Electron Sources for Future Accelerators Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in High Intensity Electron Sources for Future Accelerators 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken Our research group, based at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI), explores new technologies for future accelerator facilities. Through the development of new technologies and techniques, we develop high intensity particle sources, high gradient particle accelerators and beam diagnostics systems that measure beam qualities down to the sub-femtosecond regime. Our research combines beam/plasma physics, unique RF technologies and high-power lasers to realise the accelerators that exist within the Paul Scherrer Institute and reaching beyond with contributions to CERN’s future circular collider (FCC). This Doctoral Position will be based at PSI Villigen but with teaching assistant duties at ETH Zurich. Project background The project involves developing electron sources for future accelerator facilities at PSI and the institute’s contributions to the FCC. A central shared challenge is shaping the electron beam as it is generated or shortly afterward. For the FCC, precise control of the laser profile in the RF photogun enables the flexible filling schemes needed for top-up operation. For X-ray free-electron lasers, like SwissFEL, transverse laser shaping and early RF compression are key to producing brighter electron beams. This PhD project will advance beam-shaping techniques for both applications. Job description Commission a new electron source test stand and demonstrate pulse-to-pulse modulation of bunch charge, beam size, and laser pulse energy relevant to the FCC-ee electron source concept Compare laser-shaping techniques through beam measurements, build a prototype for photocathode operation, and investigate machine-learning/AI-based optimization to improve performance Study photocathode and laser performance, including the lifetime of semiconductor photocathodes at bunch charges of up to 5 nC Measure gains in beam brightness from both photocathode laser shaping and RF compression with applications to a SwissFEL upgrade (SwissFEL+) Profile Master’s degree (or equivalent) in physics, accelerator science, electrical engineering, photonics, or a closely related field Strong interest in accelerator physics, electron sources and experimental work; experience with beam dynamics, lasers/optics, numerical modelling or scientific programming is an advantage A practical, independent and analytical working style, combined with enthusiasm for interdisciplinary collaboration Professional proficiency in English; knowledge of German is an asset Workplace Workplace We offer We are a dynamic, interdisciplinary research group committed to innovation and collaboration. jobs.description:

We are offering two paid, full-time (100%), 3.5-year doctoral fellowships to start on October 1, 2027 . Since its inauguration, 32 scholars have been granted an A&T Fellowship. Graduates of the programme have successfully obtained academic positions at leading research institutions worldwide and high-level positions in the industry. The programme provides funding for three and a half years. It offers excellent working conditions and a unique research infrastructure. You will be employed full-time and receive monthly salaries based on a standard rate . Please find the detailed information about the doctorate at ETH Zurich in the AVETH survival guide . Project background About the Programme The A&T Doctoral Programme is ETH Zurich’s interdisciplinary educational platform committed to training scholars in research and teaching of technology in architecture. The programme is offered and managed collaboratively by the chairs of the Institute of Technology in Architecture (ITA) . jobs.title: Doctoral Position in Risk-Based Inspection and Maintenance Planning of Tunnels
jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in Risk-Based Inspection and Maintenance Planning of Tunnels Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in Risk-Based Inspection and Maintenance Planning of Tunnels 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Chair of Infrastructure Management, led by Professor Dr. Bryan T. Adey within the Institute of Construction and Infrastructure Management of the Department of Civil, Environmental and Geomatic Engineering, has an opening for a doctoral student. This position focuses risk-based inspection and maintenance planning for tunnels, including probabilistic risk updating, Value of Information analysis, and intervention program optimisation. This position is part of an interdisciplinary SNSF project in collaboration with the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano, the Hagerbach Test Gallery, and the EuroTube Foundation. The preferred starting date is 1 February 2027, although other dates are negotiable. Project background Tunnels are critical links in transport networks, and many Swiss road and rail tunnels are ageing while being subject to increasing traffic loads, climate-related stressors, and evolving safety requirements. Their maintenance involves two interdependent asset domains, namely structural elements, such as lining, portals, and drainage, and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems, such as ventilation, lighting, and fire detection. In current practice, these domains are managed largely in isolation, inspections remain heavily manual, and evidence from different campaigns, sensors, and specialists is fragmented across separate reports and databases. Interventions are therefore often planned using disjointed evidence and conservative heuristics, even where substantial data exist. The project Predictive, Resilient, Integrated Systems for Management of Tunnel (PRISM-T), funded by the SNSF, addresses this challenge through an integrated digital twin workflow for tunnel maintenance decision support. Heterogeneous inspection and monitoring evidence is transformed into uncertainty-aware condition indicators, which are used to update risk, to assess whether additional information is worth collecting, and to derive executable intervention programs. Extended reality (XR) is used to validate decisions and to guide inspection and maintenance work on site. The workflow is developed and validated in the Tunnel Digitalisation Centre of the Hagerbach Test Gallery in Flums, and its transferability is tested at the DemoTube facility of the EuroTube Foundation in Dübendorf. Regular field work at both sites and close collaboration with the partner team in Bolzano form an integral part of the doctoral research. Within this project, the doctoral position addresses the decision layer of the workflow, in which maintenance decision processes are formalised and uncertainty-aware condition indicators, developed in a companion doctoral position, are used to update risk and to optimise intervention programs under realistic tunnel constraints. Job description The successful candidate will map and formalise current tunnel maintenance decision processes for the structural and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing domains through workshops and interviews with practitioners. On this basis, risk and consequence models based on Bayesian networks will be formulated, and incremental risk updating methods will be developed. A computationally tractable Value of Information analysis will be developed using approximation strategies, such as surrogate models and scenario reduction. Intervention program optimisation models accounting for sequencing, bundling, access windows, and resource constraints will be formulated and solved, with outputs traceable to the underlying evidence. The candidate will contribute to validation campaigns at the Hagerbach Test Gallery and the EuroTube Foundation. Profile A Master’s degree in civil engineering, operations research, industrial engineering, applied mathematics, or a related field A strong background in probabilistic modelling, reliability and risk analysis, and mathematical optimisation Very good programming skills, preferably in Python, and experience with optimisation solvers Familiarity with infrastructure asset management, Bayesian networks, decision analysis, Value of Information analysis, or business process modelling would be considered an advantage Willingness to carry out field work in underground environments and to collaborate within an interdisciplinary and international team Proficiency in written and spoken English is required, and knowledge of German is regarded as an asset Workplace Workplace We offer ETH Zurich is one of the world’s leading universities specialising in science and technology. jobs.description:
Doctoral Researcher in Pulse Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Researcher in Pulse Electron Paramagnetic Resonance 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Spin Dynamics and Hyperpolarisation group is looking for a doctoral researcher, fully funded by a Starting Grant from the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF). The group explores ways to enhance the sensitivity of electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR, also known as electron spin resonance, ESR) by orders of magnitude. The project lies at the interface between method development and applied chemical spectroscopy. Starting date: by mutual agreement. There is no deadline and the position will remain open until suitable candidates are found. Applications are considered as long as this advertisement is online. Job description The position involves working with a state-of-the-art pulse EPR spectrometer with arbitrary phase and amplitude control. The aim is to develop new pulse sequences with improved sensitivity and higher information content, and to apply them to challenging systems from inorganic chemistry and catalysis, as well as to organic radicals. Our group is also developing a new method based on optical hyperpolarisation, which will eventually be applied to the same systems. The work will focus on the spectroscopic aspects, including experiments and spin-dynamics simulations. Depending on the candidate's background, it can also include chemical synthesis and catalysis, as well as quantum-chemical calculations. The working language of the group is English. Profile The candidate must hold a Master's degree in (physical) chemistry or a related field by the start of the position. Interest in spin dynamics, magnetic resonance, and their applications to (in)organic chemistry is essential. Research experience in an advanced magnetic resonance technique (EPR, solid-state NMR, or similar) is required. A good understanding of the physics underlying magnetic resonance is expected. In addition, the candidate should have: the drive to take ownership of their project and push it forward openness to collaborating with people from different backgrounds Workplace Workplace We offer An exciting project at the forefront of magnetic resonance method development A position in a new research group with close collaboration and structured mentoring Considerable freedom to pursue your own ideas and to develop both academically and personally World-class infrastructure Opportunities to initiate your own collaborations chevron_right Working, teaching and research at ETH Zurich We value diversity and sustainability In line with our values , ETH Zurich encourages an inclusive culture. jobs.title: RobotX PhD Fellowship 2027
jobs.description:
RobotX PhD Fellowship 2027 Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht RobotX PhD Fellowship 2027 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken RobotX, the Center for Robotics at ETH Zurich, is looking for outstanding doctoral students who want to build robots that work in the real world. With the RobotX PhD Fellowship 2027, you apply once and are considered by several RobotX research groups across ETH Zurich. You choose up to three professors you would like to work with, and they review your application. Application deadline: 27 November 2026. Job description The research groups of RobotX cover a broad spectrum of robotics, including but not limited to: Soft and Musculoskeletal Robotics: bioinspired robots built from compliant materials, artificial muscles, and tendons, for safe and adaptive interaction with an unstructured world. Robotic Locomotion and Manipulation: legged robots, robot arms, and hands that move and act reliably in complex terrain and contact-rich tasks. Biohybrid Robots: robots built from living cells, engineered tissue, and synthetic materials, actuated by muscle and powered by chemical energy. Perception and Computer Vision: 3D reconstruction, object recognition, and scene understanding that give robots reliable perception of their surroundings. Human-Robot Interaction: sensory-motor interaction between humans and machines for assistive, rehabilitative, and cooperative tasks. Computational Design and Fabrication: simulation, optimization, and learned surrogate models to design and fabricate efficient, bioinspired robots. Reinforcement Learning and Machine Learning: data-driven methods that let robots learn new skills and adapt to new tasks and environments. Humanoid Robotics and Tactile Sensing for Manipulation: humanoid loco-manipulation, whole-body control, and tactile sensing that let robots reason across touch and vision to handle objects dexterously. Motion Planning and Control: algorithms for navigation, control, and decision-making in dynamic environments. Safety-Critical Robotic Systems: robots that perform reliably under uncertainty, in particular when they work alongside humans. You define your doctoral project together with your supervisor during your first months. jobs.title: PhD Position in Experimental Nonlinear Dynamics and Nanomechanics
jobs.description:
PhD Position in Experimental Nonlinear Dynamics and Nanomechanics Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht PhD Position in Experimental Nonlinear Dynamics and Nanomechanics 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken We are looking for a highly motivated PhD student to join our nonlinear dynamics team. Do you have a broad interest in physics and technology? Do you like the prospect of working in an experimental project in close collaboration with theory? Are you creative, persevering, independent, and a good team player? You can expect a cutting-edge research project that is very challenging due to the many aspects of science that are involved. For the same reason, it is a highly rewarding experience if you enjoy expanding your knowledge beyond textbook physics. We look forward to meeting you! Project background Is it possible to build artificial neural networks from driven nonlinear resonators? This question builds on the ideas of Hopfield and Hinton, but takes them out of equilibrium: in our resonators, a balance of continuous drive and dissipation sustains stable oscillation states. This gives us access to phenomena that are absent in equilibrium physics. For example, this may allow us to investigate how a physical network turns stored memories into dynamical patterns. In our lab, each node is an electrical circuit or a micro-electromechanical (MEMS) resonator implementing a Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO): a driven, dissipative resonator with two stable oscillation states that act like a bit of memory. We couple several such KPOs, reading out every oscillator simultaneously and in real time. This gives us complete access to the dynamical many-body phase space. With it, we reconstruct the attractor landscape of the network, track how noise drives switching between collective states, and measure probability currents that appear when detailed balance is broken. The central question is whether these currents organize into stable, reproducible temporal patterns and coexisting limit cycles. Networks like these bridge nonequilibrium statistical physics and neuromorphic computing, and could provide a physical route to Ising and Boltzmann machines that operate on dynamical rather than static states. Job description Build and operate a programmable network of coupled KPOs with up to eight nodes, including control and readout electronics and measurement software. Map attractor landscapes, switching statistics and probability currents from measured trajectories. Compare experiment with simulations and analytical models in close contact with our theory partners (Prof. O. Zilberberg at the University of Konstanz) and publish and present your results internationally. Profile You hold (or are about to complete) an MSc in physics, electrical engineering or a related field, with a solid background in nanomechanics, nonlinear dynamics, or statistical physics. You enjoy hands-on experimental work (electronics, signal processing, Python) and are not afraid of a bit of analytical theory. Experience with MEMS, lock-in detection, or FPGAs is a plus. You communicate well in English. jobs.description:
Doctoral Position for Synthetic Biology-Inspired Therapies Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position for Synthetic Biology-Inspired Therapies 100%, Basel, fixed-term print Drucken A World-Class Research Environment at the Nexus of Biology, Engineering, and Physical Sciences The Biotechnology and Bioengineering group led by Prof. Dr. Martin Fussenegger at the Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering (D-BSSE) of the ETH Zurich in Basel invites exceptional candidates to apply for a PhD position in pioneering projects developing synthetic biology-inspired human therapies. The D-BSSE is the first truly interdisciplinary research department, uniting theoretical and experimental biology with advanced bioengineering and fostering close collaborations with leaders in material science, physics, and chemistry to drive transformative advances in systems biology, biotechnology, and synthetic biology. Situated in Basel, Switzerland, at the heart of the BioValley, a tri-national region that hosts 40% of the global life science industry and numerous major pharmaceutical companies, the D-BSSE offers a unique environment for high-impact translational research with unparalleled access to academic and industrial expertise. Project background Advancing the Frontiers of Cell-based therapies and Synthetic Biology Our group applies state-of-the-art synthetic biology principles to engineer human cells and create next-generation cell-based therapies targeting cancer as well as metabolic, neurodegenerative, autoimmune and infectious diseases. jobs.title: Doctoral Position in contact mechanics of architected interfaces
jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in contact mechanics of architected interfaces Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in contact mechanics of architected interfaces 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken At the Professorship of Solid Mechanics (SMEC) in the Institute for Building Materials at ETH Zurich, we aim to understand how materials deform, degrade, break, and ultimately fail. Our research is driven by curiosity about the physical mechanisms that underlie failure and by the ambition to translate this understanding into more reliable and resilient materials and structures. By combining numerical modeling, laboratory experiments, and theoretical analyses, we seek to link microscopic processes with the macroscopic behavior of both engineering and natural systems and develop predictive tools for mechanical failure. Our team is highly interdisciplinary and international, bringing together researchers with backgrounds in materials science, mechanics, and applied physics. We work across a broad range of topics, including the mechanics of particle systems (colloidal and granular), architected and topologically interlocked materials, the mechanics of fragility in collagen, the mechanics of earthquakes, fracture of soft materials, and modeling failure in multiphysical processes such as corrosion-driven degradation of concrete. What unites these efforts is a shared curiosity about why complex materials fail and a commitment to developing new concepts, experiments, and models that advance our understanding of failure mechanics. We are seeking a motivated and innovative doctoral student with a strong interest in solid mechanics, interface mechanics, and computational modeling to investigate how local contact interactions in architected materials shape their macroscopic interface response. The project will explore how architecture influences collective contact behavior, aiming to develop design principles. The work will combine physics-based numerical modeling, theoretical reasoning, and concepts from rough-surface and multiscale mechanics. Job description You will conduct a computational and theoretical investigation of how local contact interactions in architected materials collectively determine their macroscopic interface response. The work will connect cell-scale mechanics with concepts from multiscale/rough-surface contact mechanics to develop effective descriptions of architected interfaces. You will develop and use numerical models of lattice materials to investigate the underlying principles of contact behavior of architected materials. You will analyze how architectural features, material properties, and characteristic length scales influence quantities such as contact area, pressure distributions, interface stiffness, and load transmission. Building on these results, you will seek statistical or homogenized descriptions that connect the mechanics of individual contacting cells to the effective behavior of large architected interfaces. The position provides a stimulating environment for scientific growth and collaboration. Profile You hold an MSc degree in mechanics, physics, (civil, mechanical, aerospace, or bio-) engineering, material science, computational science, or a related discipline. You have a background in mechanics, applied physics, computational mechanics, scientific computing, or a related field. A foundation in areas such as solid mechanics, contact mechanics, or multiscale modeling is particularly relevant. You have experience implementing scientific code and assessing computational results through validation, verification, and quantitative comparison with reference data. You have prior programming experience in Python and have used version control. You are curious, self-motivated, and interested in using modeling and quantitative reasoning to answer mechanics and physics questions. Experience with architected materials, rough-surface contact mechanics, homogenization, statistical mechanics, or multiscale methods is an advantage but is not required; the project-specific methods and concepts can be learned during the doctoral studies. You are fluent in English (oral and written). You enjoy working in a team, possess the necessary social skills and communication abilities, and contribute proactively to a positive group atmosphere. jobs.title: Doctoral Student in Neuromotor Interfaces for Dexterous Robot Teleoperation (multimodal egocentric vision + EMG)
jobs.description:
Doctoral Student in Neuromotor Interfaces for Dexterous Robot Teleoperation (multimodal egocentric vision + EMG) Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Student in Neuromotor Interfaces for Dexterous Robot Teleoperation (multimodal egocentric vision + EMG) 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab invites applications for a fully funded PhD position at ETH Zürich at the intersection of robotics, wearable sensing, signal processing, machine learning, and human-computer interaction. The goal of this PhD is to develop neuromotor interfaces for dexterous robot teleoperation using two sensing modalities: 1) surface electromyography (sEMG) measured at the wrist or forearm, with the aim of decoding subtle hand and finger activity, continuous movement, and motor intent in real time. 2) egocentric vision as a complementary input channel. While EMG provides information about human motor intent, egocentric cameras can provide context about the surrounding scene, manipulated objects, hand–object interactions, and task state. Combining these modalities creates opportunities for interfaces that understand both what the user intends to do and what is happening in the environment. The PhD will focus on the computational and sensing methods required to make such systems robust, generalizable, and effective in real interactive settings, including multimodal learning and reasoning across neuromotor and egocentric visual signals , while exploring applications in Mixed Reality and other interactive systems. Particularly beneficial: You have a background in (or experience with) prototyping sensing systems ( embedded systems , signal acquisition, processing, PCBs) Note: This is not a position in biomedical engineering and there is no health focus. Project background Wearable EMG provides a direct and unobtrusive way to sense muscle activity underlying hand and finger movements. This creates opportunities for interfaces that can recognize subtle actions, continuously estimate movement, and infer motor intent before or without large observable movements. Making such interfaces work reliably outside controlled settings remains a substantial research problem. EMG varies across users and recording sessions and is sensitive to electrode placement, contact conditions, movement, and other sources of noise. This motivates research in signal processing, temporal machine learning, representation learning, adaptation, and real-time inference. A second challenge is that neuromotor signals alone provide limited information about what the user is interacting with and why a particular movement is occurring. The project will therefore combine EMG with egocentric vision to capture objects, hands, contacts, affordances, and task state. This creates a multimodal research problem: learning representations that combine neuromotor and visual information and developing methods for reasoning about human intent, hand–object interaction, and the state of an ongoing manipulation task. For robotic teleoperation, these multimodal signals can support systems that jointly reason about what action the user intends, which object or target the action refers to, and how that intent should be translated to a robot with a different embodiment. Relevant problems include dexterous manipulation, shared autonomy, multimodal intent inference, and reasoning over sequences of human and robot actions. Job description Develop signal-processing and machine-learning methods for multichannel EMG, including discrete and continuous decoding of hand and finger activity Develop egocentric computer-vision methods for understanding hands, objects, hand–object interactions, contacts, affordances, and task state Develop multimodal learning and reasoning methods that combine EMG with egocentric vision to infer motor intent and interaction context Investigate reasoning over objects, actions, interaction sequences, and task state to resolve ambiguous motor signals and anticipate intended actions Apply methods to dexterous robot teleoperation , including mapping human motor intent to robot manipulators and dexterous hands optionally: Prototype wearable sensing systems , including electrode configurations, signal acquisition, embedded processing, and hardware and software integration (huge plus) Develop and evaluate applications in robotics, Mixed Reality , and other interactive systems and as in each PhD Disseminate your findings in publications at top-tier venues and open-source research results and tools where appropriate Present research findings at academic conferences, workshops, and seminars Profile ETH requirements: written and spoken fluency in English an excellent master's degree (MSc., M.Eng. or equivalent) in Computer Science, Electrical Engineering, Robotics, or related field You bring: A strong foundation in machine learning , including classification and regression, model evaluation, representation learning, and generalization A solid understanding of signals and time-series data (e.g., sampling, frequency, phase, noise, spectral representations, and filtering) Strong programming skills and experience implementing and quantitatively evaluating computational methods An interest in building real-time sensing and interactive systems , including experimentation with physical sensors A strong background in one or more of the following areas is particularly beneficial: Electrical engineering and signal processing: EMG or other electrophysiological signals, sensor systems, embedded systems, electronics, or wearable sensing Robotics: manipulation, dexterous manipulation, teleoperation, robot learning, shared autonomy, or human-robot interaction Computer Vision: egocentric vision, hand and object pose estimation, hand–object interaction, contact and affordance estimation, video understanding, or action recognition Machine learning: temporal modeling, representation learning, multimodal learning, multimodal reasoning , domain adaptation, or learning from noisy sensor data Interactive systems: HCI, Mixed Reality, wearable computing, or real-time input systems We do not expect applicants to already be experts across all of these areas. You will have the opportunity to develop complete research systems spanning wearable sensing, egocentric perception, machine learning, and robotic interaction . In our research, we frequently collaborate with other groups and departments as well as institutions and companies in Switzerland and abroad. During your PhD, you will have the opportunity to contribute to and collaborate with the ETH AI Center and engage in ETHAR, ETH's Research Hub for Augmented Reality in collaboration with Google XR . The position provides access to infrastructure for wearable and embedded prototyping, egocentric sensing, interactive systems, and robotic manipulation. jobs.title: Doctoral Positions in Robot Learning and Soft, Musculoskeletal, and Biohybrid Robotics
jobs.description:
Doctoral Positions in Robot Learning and Soft, Musculoskeletal, and Biohybrid Robotics Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Positions in Robot Learning and Soft, Musculoskeletal, and Biohybrid Robotics 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Soft Robotics Lab within the Institute of Robotics and Intelligent Systems at ETH Zurich is inviting applications for several doctoral positions. Our lab's goal is to build, model, and control robots in a fundamentally different way, so that they become more flexible, dexterous, capable, and adapt better to their environment. We work along four directions: soft and musculoskeletal robotics, biohybrid living systems, dexterous manipulation and robot learning, and simulation for embodied AI. We are looking for exceptional candidates in any of them. This round we especially want two profiles: people who design and build the robots, and people who make policies run on them. We do not hire against a narrow project description. Your thesis topic is something we shape together in your first months. Tell us which of our directions pulls at you, and what you would want to build. Project background Today's robots are mostly rigid, fragile, and a world apart from the agility and resilience of biological bodies. Our bet is that the next generation of robots will be soft, musculoskeletal, and in part alive. They will be built to make contact with the real world rather than to avoid it. We pursue this across four directions, and a strong candidate will find a home in one of them and borrow from the others. Soft and musculoskeletal robotics. We build bodies from compliant structures, bones, joints, and tendon-like actuation. Our electrohydraulic musculoskeletal leg jumps, moves fast, and adapts to terrain at roughly 1.2% of the energy a motor-driven leg needs ( Nature Communications, 2024 ). Our low-voltage HASEL actuators run near 1100 V, are safe to touch, and work untethered and underwater ( Science Advances, 2024 ). We recently extended these muscles to full antagonistic motion ranges ( ICRA 2025 ) and to a sensorless, inherently compliant anthropomorphic hand driven entirely by electrohydraulic actuation ( IROS 2026 ). Biohybrid living systems. We grow engineered muscle and use it to actuate machines. We bioprinted multicellular muscle-tendon units that transmit force along a real musculoskeletal path ( Science Advances, 2025 ), embedded sensors directly into muscle for closed-loop control of proprioceptive biohybrid robots ( Advanced Intelligent Systems, 2025 ), and established functional volumetric bioprinting with xolography ( Advanced Materials, 2026 ). Co-optimized volumetric muscle designs for large dynamic deformations are in press at Nature Communications (Balciunaite et al., 2026). The same fabrication line reaches clinical work: with University Hospital Zurich we printed implantable reinforced cardiac tissue patches ( Advanced Materials, 2025 ). Dexterous manipulation and robot learning. We build hands and the policies that run them. One of our initial hand designs is now commercialized through our spin-off Mimic Robotics . ORCA is our open-source, reliable, and cost-effective anthropomorphic hand for uninterrupted dexterous task learning ( IROS 2025 ). On that hardware we work on imitation learning and diffusion policies, cross-embodiment skill transfer through latent action diffusion (ICRA 2026), sample-efficient reinforcement learning and policy fine-tuning directly on the real robot , vision-language-action models for contact-rich tasks, and tactile representation learning on our high-resolution sensorized skin (ICRA 2024). We also build controllable dexterous world models for training and evaluation, and a benchmark of dexterity for anthropomorphic hands . Whichever side you come from, the offer is the same: the hand, the skin, the simulator, and the people who designed all three sit in one room. Build a mechanism here and someone will have a policy running on it within weeks. Build a policy here and you can change the mechanism when the mechanism is what is wrong. Simulation, fabrication, and embodied AI. Building these robots requires tools that did not exist. Vision-Controlled Jetting prints rigid skeletons, soft tissue, tendons, and sensors in one pass, including a full musculoskeletal hand and forearm ( Nature, 2023 ). We close the sim-to-real gap with learned residual physics ( RA-L, 2024, Best Paper Award ), and we released SORS , a modular high-fidelity soft-robot simulator, at RoboSoft 2026. Underwater and aerial systems run through all of this, from SoFi and tendon-driven swimmer digital twins to our open-source soft aerial manipulation platform ( CoRL 2024 ). Job description Depending on your direction, your work will emphasize different parts of the following. All of it happens in a lab where hardware, biology, and learning sit in the same room. You will take a research idea from concept to a working system: designing the architecture, building it, integrating sensing and control, and validating it through systematic real-world experiments If your focus is systems design, you will design and build the robots themselves: mechanisms and compliant structures, actuators and tendon routing, embedded electronics and motor control, and the sensor integration that makes a machine measurable. You will own a system from CAD through fabrication to hardware that still runs six months later If your focus is learning, you will develop policies and perception that run on real, compliant, contact-rich hardware: imitation learning, real-world reinforcement learning and fine-tuning, sim-to-real transfer, and multimodal representations that use touch as well as vision. You will help define the benchmarks that make such claims measurable Each design cycle feeds the next, so rapid prototyping, measurement, and iteration sit at the heart of every project Drawing inspiration from biological musculoskeletal systems, you will engineer how bones, joints, tendons, and muscles can be recreated with compliant materials, artificial actuators, or living tissue, and how their interplay produces strength, dexterity, and robustness You will build robots that derive much of their capability from their embodiment, achieving rich, adaptive behavior with less reliance on complex centralized control If your focus is biohybrid systems, you will work in our biological laboratories at ETH, culturing and bioprinting tissue and turning it into a controllable actuator You will publish at the top venues in the field, release open-source hardware and code where it helps the community, and present your work internationally You will supervise semester and Master's projects, which is how most of our doctoral students learn to lead work, and you will collaborate day to day across our hardware, muscles, and machine learning teams You will complete a doctorate at ETH Zurich alongside the research, including the coursework of the D-MAVT doctoral programme and a share of teaching in one of our courses Profile You are curious, highly motivated, and independent, and you want to make a real difference with your research You work best in a team. You are respectful, and you thrive when you can collaborate with others and support them Through your prior experience, you have ideally already demonstrated: A completed or nearly completed Master's degree in mechanical engineering, robotics, mechatronics, electrical engineering, computer science, materials science, bioengineering, or a closely related field Depth in at least one of: hands-on system building and mechatronics (CAD, FEA, 3D printing, machining, molding, electronics, motor control, robot integration), machine learning and control for real robots, soft or bio-inspired materials and actuators, tissue engineering and biofabrication, or physics-based simulation Evidence that you carry work through to reality.
